event: The Mac reboots (power cut, macOS update, crash) and the server stays down until someone logs in on the Mac.
trigger: Power cut, automatic macOS update, a crash or a lid-closed sleep. The server is a LaunchAgent, which only starts after the user 'worker' logs in; the plist's own comment says a reboot needs auto-login first.
cost: App dead for hours to days, every scan fails, new subscribers see errors. Time depends on whether Jamin is home.
detect: The GitHub alarm emails Jamin after two failed probes (about 1 hour). Not checked: whether Jamin reads that email quickly, and whether auto-login is on today.
response: 1. Get to the Mac (or a person at home) and log in as worker. 2. Confirm /api/health answers. 3. Turn on auto-login or move the server to a system-level job so it starts without a login.
smallest_fix: Reboot the Mac once on purpose and see whether the server returns by itself; if not, enable auto-login (see blind-18 for the FileVault clash) or run the server as a boot-time job.

event: Home internet goes down, the router or ISP changes, or the tunnel process dies, so the public address answers an error (Cloudflare 530).
trigger: ISP outage, router reset, new modem, cloudflared crash or a stale cloudflared version Cloudflare stops supporting.
cost: App dead for the length of the outage. Today (2026-11-18 17:50 UTC) a mailbox message from the Mac reported HTTP 530 on the public health check, so this is not hypothetical.
detect: GitHub alarm email after two failed probes; Mac job reports through the mailbox (seen today, header only, cause not read).
response: 1. Check the Mac has internet. 2. Restart the tunnel job. 3. If it is the ISP, wait or tether the Mac to a phone. 4. Confirm health answers.
smallest_fix: Write a five-line outage runbook (what a 530 means, how to restart the tunnel, how to tether) and rehearse it once by unplugging the router.

event: The Mac itself dies or is lost (disk failure, battery, liquid, theft) and all live data goes with it.
trigger: Hardware failure of a laptop run as a server, or theft from home. Nightly backups sit on the same disk and are unencrypted.
cost: All scan history, shopper corrections, caches and the 3.5 GB catalogue gone; days of rebuild; app down meanwhile. Entitlements survive (RevenueCat holds them).
detect: The alarm would show the server down, but nothing says the backups are gone too.
response: 1. Get any Mac, install Node, clone the repo. 2. Restore the latest backup from wherever a copy survives. 3. Rebuild the catalogue and prices from the import scripts. 4. Repoint the tunnel.
smallest_fix: Copy the nightly backup somewhere off the machine (the config example mentions a Dropbox folder; whether it is really used was not checked) and do one restore on the PC from that copy.
fix_cost: 2 hours, 0 to 5 dollars a month for storage

event: The backup job fails or the Mac disk fills up, and nobody is told; the server then fails on writes or the next restore is empty or old.
trigger: Disk full from 14 backup copies, the 6 GB weekly price download, unrotated log files and growing scan tables; or the backup script errors.
cost: Silent loss of the safety net; a full disk can stop every write and the server. A restore day finds the last good copy is weeks old.
detect: Nobody would know. The disk guard covers photos only (2 GB floor); no backup-failure alarm was found in the repo (not found, not proven absent). The backup script lives in the Mac's ~/bin and is not in the repo.
response: 1. Check free space and the newest backup file date. 2. Delete old downloads and logs. 3. Re-run the backup by hand.
smallest_fix: Add the newest-backup age and free disk space to /api/health and make the GitHub alarm go red when the backup is over 36 hours old or free space is under 10 GB.

event: The relay.anjiawenda.com domain lapses, is transferred, or its registrar email goes to someone nobody checks; every installed app stops working at once.
trigger: Expiry date passes, card on file fails, registrar account owner is not Jamin or Aurik, or the owner sells or loses it.
cost: Total outage of every installed build with no server-side fix: the host name is baked into the binary, so recovery means a new App Store release plus waiting for users to update. Loses most users who give up.
detect: Nobody would know until the probe failed; the cause (domain) would then take time to find. The owner and renewal date are recorded as unknown.
response: 1. Find the registrar and log in. 2. Renew or recover the domain. 3. If lost, ship a build that points at a new host.
smallest_fix: Find out who owns the domain and the renewal date today, turn on auto-renew with a card that will not expire, add the date to a calendar, and put a second contact email on it.
fix_cost: 30 minutes, about 15 to 25 dollars a year

event: The Cloudflare account has a problem (locked login, free-plan limit, revoked tunnel token, billing or abuse flag) and the tunnel stops.
trigger: Lost two-factor device, a Cloudflare policy change, the tunnel token deleted by accident, or a spike that Cloudflare throttles.
cost: Same as an outage; recovery depends on regaining a vendor account that has no named backup owner.
detect: Alarm email once probes fail; the cause would not be obvious.
response: 1. Log in to Cloudflare and read the tunnel status. 2. Recreate the tunnel and token if needed. 3. Update the Mac job.
smallest_fix: Write down where the Cloudflare login and recovery codes are kept and give Aurik emergency access.

event: The alarm email never reaches a person in time (spam folder, Jamin busy at exams or work, or GitHub's free Actions minutes run out) and an outage runs for days.
trigger: The alarm runs at 48 probes a day plus retries; a private repo on the free plan has a monthly minute allowance that this may approach. The failure email goes to one inbox and there is no phone push.
cost: Each day of unseen downtime loses first-week users; a quota stop turns the alarm off silently.
detect: Nobody would know if the alarm itself stops. Not checked: repo visibility, the minutes used, or where the email lands.
response: 1. Check the Actions tab and billing page. 2. Cut the schedule to every 60 minutes if near the quota. 3. Add a second recipient.
smallest_fix: Open GitHub billing to see minutes used; add a second alert channel (a phone push or Aurik's email) and an outside dead-man ping that complains when the alarm stops running.

event: The server is up but giving wrong or empty answers (catalogue not attached, no prices, a broken lookup) and the alarm stays green.
trigger: The catalogue file fails to attach after a restart, a data import goes wrong, a bad deploy changes answers. The probe checks door behaviour and treats a 400 on a POST as a pass; it does not read the health fields (catalogueUp, pricesHealth, scanLog, faultHealth).
cost: Every scan returns 'no price' or a wrong verdict for days; reviews turn bad; refunds and churn.
detect: Nobody would know. The health endpoint holds the signals but nothing reads them.
response: 1. Open /api/health and read the failing field. 2. Restart the server or roll back. 3. Reload the data.
smallest_fix: Make the alarm fail when catalogueUp is false, pricesHealth is bad or fault counts jump, and add one real known-barcode scan that must return a price.

event: The monthly Claude cap (1,000 calls) or the Anthropic credit balance runs out, or the key is revoked; price estimates quietly stop.
trigger: A viral week, a script hitting the estimate path, an expired card or empty prepaid balance, or a key rotated by mistake.
cost: Shoppers who agreed to an estimate see 'no estimate' on the scans that most need it; the line in the brief says it 'alerts loudly' but the cap message goes to the server log only, which no person reads.
detect: Nobody would know. claudeMonthlyCap appears in /api/health; errors go to stderr only.
response: 1. Check the Anthropic console for balance and key status. 2. Top up or raise the cap with a stated limit. 3. Confirm one estimate works.
smallest_fix: Email Jamin once when usage passes 80 percent of the cap, and set Anthropic's own spend limit and low-balance email on the account.
sources: app/server.ts (claudeCapHealth near line 1668); identify/src/range-ask.ts; app/src/errlog.ts; RULINGS.md Model spend cap

event: Anthropic retires the hard-coded model (claude-haiku-4-5-20251001) and the estimate path starts failing.
trigger: A model deprecation notice sent to the account email; the model name is fixed in code.
cost: Estimates stop until a deploy; the circuit breaker opens and hides the failure.
detect: Nobody would know except by the Anthropic notice email, whose reader is not set.
response: 1. Read the notice. 2. Change the model name in one place. 3. Deploy and test one estimate.
smallest_fix: Put the model name in server config, and write the Anthropic deprecation date in the calendar when the notice comes.

event: RevenueCat is slow or down, its secret key is rotated, or the lookup limiter is hit during a spike, so paying subscribers are treated as free.
trigger: A RevenueCat incident right after a server restart (the cache is in memory and the fallback is last-known-else-free), a wrong or expired REVENUECAT_SECRET_KEY, or more than 120 lookups a minute.
cost: People who paid hit the free limit; complaints and refund requests; Plus looks broken in the first week.
detect: Nobody would know; a failing lookup is only a log line.
response: 1. Check RevenueCat status and the key. 2. Restart after RevenueCat recovers so the cache refills. 3. Tell affected users to tap Restore Purchases.
smallest_fix: Count failed entitlement lookups in /api/health and alarm on a streak; when the lookup fails and the user was Plus within the last day, keep them Plus.

event: A paying user writes 'I paid but it says free' (new phone, reinstall, Keychain not restored, Apple ID switch) and there is nobody to answer or a clear fix path.
trigger: The device id lives in the Keychain and localStorage; a changed phone or wiped app can lose it. Restore Purchases is on the You screen.
cost: One lost subscriber and a bad review each time; refund requests to Apple.
detect: Only if the support inbox is read (see blind-14).
response: 1. Reply with the Restore Purchases steps. 2. If it fails, look the customer up in RevenueCat. 3. Grant access by hand or point them to an Apple refund.
smallest_fix: Write a short canned reply and the RevenueCat lookup steps, then run through one fake case.

event: Apple refunds, chargebacks or subscription cancellations pile up unseen, or an App Store review wave (good or bad) goes unanswered for weeks.
trigger: Normal subscription churn, a bad week of wrong prices, a rating dip after launch. Apple lets developers reply to reviews; nobody is assigned.
cost: Rating below about 4 cuts installs; unanswered complaints cost conversions. Hard to size, likely the largest slow leak.
detect: Nobody would know; reviews appear only in App Store Connect, which nobody is named to open.
response: 1. Open App Store Connect reviews weekly. 2. Reply to the real problems within 2 days. 3. Fix repeated causes.
smallest_fix: Name Aurik or Jamin as weekly reviewer, set a recurring calendar slot, and turn on Apple's review email notices.

event: The support email (useshinapp@gmail.com, old Shin name) gets messages nobody reads, including French messages, bug reports and legal requests with a 30-day clock.
trigger: Any user, journalist, retailer or lawyer writes in. Who reads the inbox is unknown. Jamin's internship starts May 3, 2027.
cost: Missed privacy request deadlines (statutory 30 days), lost subscribers, a missed press or partner reply. The old name is also the name Jamin banned from public view.
detect: Nobody would know; no forwarding or auto-reply is recorded.
response: 1. Pick one reader per week. 2. Reply in the user's language within 2 days. 3. Log privacy requests with their deadline.
smallest_fix: Decide the reader, set a phone alert on that inbox, add a short auto-reply with the expected response time, and switch the public address to a Pexi-named one that forwards to it.
fix_cost: 1 hour, 0 to 8 dollars a month for a custom address

event: A privacy request arrives (see my data, delete it, withdraw consent) and the person cannot be matched to a phone because there are no accounts.
trigger: A user or the Privacy Commissioner writes in; Quebec Law 25 and PIPEDA both set 30-day clocks.
cost: A regulator complaint or fine risk if ignored; hours of manual database work if done late.
detect: Only through the support inbox (blind-14).
response: 1. Ask the user to read their device id from the You screen. 2. Run the removal steps in the data-requests doc. 3. Reply with what was removed and when.
smallest_fix: Run the procedure once end to end on a test phone and time it.

event: The nightly retention cleanup quietly stops working, or the data kept in backups and log files outlives what the privacy policy promises.
trigger: The cleanup runs only inside the server on a 24-hour timer and reports failure only to the log. The server's own log files and the 14 backup copies have no recorded rotation or purge for deleted rows (not found, not proven absent).
cost: The policy says 12 months, 24 months and 90 days; keeping more is a broken promise in a regulator or breach review.
detect: Nobody would know; a failed sweep is a stderr line.
response: 1. Read the log for 'retention' errors. 2. Run the sweep by hand. 3. Trim old logs and aged backups.
smallest_fix: Put the last successful sweep time in /api/health and alarm if over 3 days; add log rotation to the Mac.

event: A data breach or leaked secret (stolen Mac, leaked RevenueCat, Anthropic or App Store Connect key, exposed backup) needs notice to people and the regulator.
trigger: The Mac has FileVault and the firewall off, backups are unencrypted, and the keys sit on that machine.
cost: Mandatory notification work, possible fines, loss of trust; key abuse bills if a key leaks.
detect: Only if the thief or attacker announces it; there is no intrusion or leak alert.
response: 1. Rotate every key. 2. Follow the breach plan steps and its notice templates. 3. Notify within the stated time.
smallest_fix: Do a 30 minute tabletop of the breach plan with Aurik and list every key with where to rotate it.

event: The planned fix for a stolen or lost Mac (turn on FileVault) breaks the planned fix for reboots (auto-login), so the server stays down after every restart until someone types the disk password.
trigger: macOS does not allow automatic login while FileVault is on. Both fixes are on the findings lists. This is a known Apple behaviour; I did not test it on this Mac.
cost: Fixing one risk makes the other worse; a reboot while Jamin is away means a long outage.
detect: Fixing is where it appears; after the change an unplanned reboot leaves the server down (alarm email only).
response: 1. Decide which risk to take. 2. If FileVault: run the server as a system-level job and plan how to unlock after a reboot. 3. Rehearse a reboot once.
smallest_fix: Write down the chosen trade-off (FileVault on with manual unlock, or off with a stated named cost) before changing either setting.

event: Someone scripts the API (a bot, a competitor, a curious developer), burning Claude calls, filling disk with photos or corrections, or starving real users.
trigger: A public hostname baked into a free app; limits are per address and in memory, so a restart clears them and a rotating address list bypasses them.
cost: Claude cap used up (blind-09), disk fills (blind-04), slow answers for everyone.
detect: Only the door limiter's own 429s; nothing reports them.
response: 1. Read the request log for the heavy address or path. 2. Block it at Cloudflare. 3. Lower the limit on the abused route.
smallest_fix: Add a daily count of 429s and Claude calls per address to a weekly numbers email; write the Cloudflare block steps.
sources: app/src/rate-limit.ts; app/server.ts lines 906 to 1010 and 1624 to 1644

event: Many real shoppers share one internet address (mobile carrier shared addresses, a campus or store wifi) and hit the per-address free scan or door limit, so honest users see 'slow down' errors.
trigger: The limits count by the address Cloudflare reports. Canadian carriers often put many phones behind one address; an in-store or campus launch concentrates users.
cost: Honest users blocked and blaming the app; bad reviews that cannot be reproduced.
detect: Nobody would know; the 429s are not counted anywhere.
response: 1. Read the 429 counts per address. 2. Raise the per-address limit or move the free limit to the device id. 3. Tell affected users.
smallest_fix: Log blocked addresses with the device id, and make the free quota follow the device id rather than the address.

event: A good event: Pexi goes viral (a TikTok, a news story, a grocery-price moment) and traffic jumps 50 times in a day on one laptop at home.
trigger: Press, a viral video, an Apple feature, a back-to-school or inflation news cycle.
cost: The laptop, the home internet, the door limit (15,000 a day), RevenueCat's lookup limit and the Claude cap all hit at once; first-day users see errors and never come back, wasting the best acquisition day.
detect: The alarm would see failures, but not the rise before them.
response: 1. Check load and the limits. 2. Raise limits and the Claude cap for the day. 3. Move the server to a rented machine if it lasts.
smallest_fix: Write a 'spike' page with the dial for each limit, and test the server with a simple load script at 20 times normal traffic.

event: A free map or product data service throttles or blocks the Mac (OpenStreetMap Overpass, Open Food Facts), or an OFF outage is remembered as 'product not found'.
trigger: The Overpass request says 'six testers' in its User-Agent and Open Food Facts is called with no User-Agent; both services ask clients to identify themselves and may limit by home address. OFF misses are cached.
cost: Store lookups and unknown-barcode names fail for everyone; wrong 'not found' results linger.
detect: Nobody would know; fallbacks are not alarmed.
response: 1. Check whether the source answers from the Mac. 2. Clear the cached misses. 3. Switch to the fallback or contact the service.
smallest_fix: Send a proper User-Agent with a real contact address, do not cache errors as misses, and count source failures in /api/health.

event: The weekly Project Hammer price refresh fails or the source disappears, so prices go stale week after week.
trigger: One hobbyist download address; a changed file format; a full disk (needs about 6 GB); the Sunday job not running.
cost: Verdicts based on old prices; the shown prices drift from the shelf; trust loss over weeks.
detect: The GitHub alarm goes red when the last refresh is over 8 days old and emails Jamin.
response: 1. Run the refresh script by hand and read the error. 2. If the source is gone, mark prices as older and look for another source. 3. Tell Aurik.
response_exists: yes: mac/hammer-refresh.sh (the script only; no runbook found)
smallest_fix: Wait for the first scheduled Sunday run, confirm it moved the mark, and write a short 'refresh failed' runbook.
sources: scripts/data-freshness.mjs; mac/hammer-refresh.sh; mac/launchd/com.shin.hammer.plist; price/src/hammer.ts lines 340 to 360

event: The weekly refresh succeeds but the data is wrong (a unit change, prices 100 times off, a half-empty file) and shoppers see wrong verdicts.
trigger: A change in the source's data. The import deletes the earlier matched and loose rows and rewrites them in one step; no count or price sanity check was found (a search found nothing, not proof).
cost: 'Great price' on a bad one, or the reverse, across many products; reviews and refunds; the freshness alarm stays green.
detect: Nobody would know; the mark only says the job finished.
response: 1. Compare this week's counts and median price to last week. 2. Restore the previous database from backup. 3. Re-run after the source is fixed.
smallest_fix: Before marking a refresh done, refuse it if product count drops over 30 percent or the median price moves over 20 percent; keep last week's data.

event: A retailer, brand or data provider writes in (complaint about a shown price, a request to stop using their data, a new terms notice or an expired key for a source such as Icecat or the BC liquor feed) and we need to switch the source off or remove its rows quickly.
trigger: Any such message to the support inbox or an account email; sources also have accounts, keys and terms that change.
cost: Days lost finding how to do it; an escalation if ignored. Only operational handling is covered here, not legal opinion.
detect: Only through the support inbox (blind-14) or the source's account email.
response: 1. Reply to acknowledge within 2 days. 2. Switch the source off and remove its rows. 3. Confirm to the sender.
smallest_fix: Write and test a one-command 'remove every row from seller X and switch the source off' (a per-seller removal command was not found; only matched-row and shopper-row removal exist).

event: Shoppers type prices, names or photos that are junk, rude, deliberately false or private (faces, children), and that content shapes verdicts or sits on the server.
trigger: Open text and photo fields in a 4+ app; no profanity or abuse filter was found (not found, not proven absent).
cost: Wrong verdicts for a barcode, an embarrassing name in an answer, private photos kept up to the retention window, an Apple complaint.
detect: Nobody would know; there is no review queue or report alert.
response: 1. Look up the barcode's shopper rows. 2. Remove them with the removal script. 3. Turn off typed prices with the switch if it spreads.
response_exists: yes: scripts/security/remove-shopper-input.mjs (header describes the switch SHIN_SHOPPER_VOICE=off)
smallest_fix: Run the removal script once on test data, and list a weekly top-10 of most-edited barcodes to scan by eye.

event: Apple rejects the first public version or a later update (metadata, privacy label, subscription wording, screenshots), and a fix is stuck in a multi-day review loop.
trigger: Any submission. Apple writes to the developer account email and the resolution centre; who watches them is not recorded.
cost: Launch slips days; an urgent fix is stuck behind review; momentum from any launch push is lost.
detect: Apple's email and App Store Connect; only if someone reads them.
response: 1. Read the reason in the resolution centre. 2. Fix and reply the same day. 3. Resubmit.
smallest_fix: Make sure the Apple account email reaches both Aurik and Jamin on a phone, and keep a list of past rejection causes.
sources: docs/store/listing.md; RULINGS.md App id and App Store sections

event: The Apple Developer Program membership lapses (annual renewal, expired card) and the app disappears from the store.
trigger: Annual renewal date unremembered; the account is an individual account in Jamin's legal name; the card on file expires.
cost: App removed, new downloads stop, builds cannot be submitted; renewal itself is the annual fee, but the lost days cost installs.
detect: Apple emails the account holder before and after; no calendar date is recorded.
response: 1. Pay the renewal. 2. Confirm the app is live again. 3. Re-check certificates.
smallest_fix: Put the renewal date and a 30-day-before reminder in the calendar, and turn on auto-renew.

event: Apple holds updates or pays nothing until paperwork is fixed (new agreement to accept, bank or tax form, Canadian GST/HST condition), and first payouts never arrive.
trigger: Apple posts a new agreement or the banking, tax or GST/HST details are incomplete. The legal review lists the GST/HST condition and business registration items; whether they are done is not recorded.
cost: Revenue held (first payout comes weeks after the first month closes); updates blocked until the account holder accepts.
detect: Apple's banner in App Store Connect and an email; nobody is set to read it.
response: 1. Log in as the account holder. 2. Accept or complete the form. 3. Check the payout status.
smallest_fix: Open Agreements, Tax and Banking once and list every item still open; put a monthly check on the calendar.

event: The Apple Small Business Program enrolment is missed or not renewed, so Apple keeps 30 percent instead of 15 percent of every sale.
trigger: Enrolment is a separate step, checked each year against the revenue limit. It is mentioned in decisions.md; no record that it was applied for was found.
cost: 15 points of revenue on each subscription (about 60 cents on a 3.99 month, 4.50 on a 29.99 year).
detect: Only by reading the payout statement; nobody is assigned.
response: 1. Apply in App Store Connect. 2. Confirm the status is Enrolled. 3. Re-check each November.
smallest_fix: Check enrolment status today and enrol if not done.

event: The first real income arrives and the business paperwork is not ready (Ontario business name registration, sole-proprietor income reporting, GST/HST small-supplier decision, a business bank account).
trigger: Apple payouts begin; the legal review lists these as open.
cost: Penalties and interest if late; messy books for tax time; the legal name shown on the store page is already a privacy concern.
detect: Only a tax deadline or a letter; nobody is assigned.
response: 1. Register the business name. 2. Open a separate account. 3. Track revenue and costs monthly. 4. Book an accountant for the first filing.
smallest_fix: One accountant call and a shared monthly sheet of income and costs.
fix_cost: 2 hours, accountant fee (a few hundred dollars)

event: Apple's age-rating questionnaire has a dated deadline (2027-01-12) and the app cannot be updated if it is not re-answered, with alcohol-price data and open text in a 4+ app being a likely point of change.
trigger: Apple's re-answer requirement; the date is in the launch checklist.
cost: Updates blocked on the day a fix is needed; a possible higher rating that changes who may download.
detect: The date is in the launch checklist; there is no calendar alarm recorded.
response: 1. Open the questionnaire in App Store Connect. 2. Answer for what the app actually shows. 3. Save and note the result.
smallest_fix: Do it this week and write the answers down.

event: The distribution certificate, provisioning profile or the App Store Connect API key expires, and the next build or release cannot be made when an urgent fix is needed.
trigger: Certificates last about a year; the signing runs on the Mac with its own key.
cost: An urgent fix delayed by a day or more while signing is rebuilt.
detect: Only when a build fails.
response: 1. Read the Xcode error. 2. Renew the certificate or key. 3. Rebuild.
smallest_fix: List certificate and key expiry dates and put them in the calendar.
sources: RULINGS.md (App Store Connect key on the Mac); native/README.md

event: Jamin or Aurik is locked out of a vendor account (Apple ID, GitLab, GitHub, Cloudflare, RevenueCat, Anthropic, the domain registrar) because the single two-factor phone or recovery email is lost.
trigger: A lost or broken phone, a changed number, an unread recovery email on a closed account.
cost: Days with no way to change the server, the app or billing; Apple recovery can take weeks.
detect: At the moment it is needed.
response: 1. Use the stored recovery codes. 2. Start the vendor's recovery flow. 3. Ask the other partner to act if they have access.
smallest_fix: Print the recovery codes, store them somewhere other than the phone, and list who can act on each account.

event: A deploy passes the tests but ships a harmful change (wrong answers, a bad data migration, a slow route), and rollback is only automatic for mechanical failures.
trigger: A push to main by Jamin, Aurik or a Claude session; tests cannot see answer quality.
cost: Hours of wrong verdicts live before anyone notices (see blind-08).
detect: The alarm only if the door breaks; otherwise a user message.
response: 1. Send the pin command through the mailbox to freeze on the last good build. 2. Revert the commit on the PC. 3. Release.
tried: yes: 2026-11-17 deploy checked end to end (per the brief; pin and hold not shown tried)
smallest_fix: Practise one pin and release cycle and one revert, and write the time it takes.

event: The deploy path stalls (GitLab outage or token expiry, the mailbox repo breaks, the checker job stops) and a fix cannot be shipped, with only a quiet heartbeat to say so.
trigger: The Mac polls GitLab as @jaminke and takes 'deploy:' commands through the PC-Mac mailbox; its heartbeat reports GONE QUIET after 60 minutes, as shown in today's session header for other jobs.
cost: A needed fix is stuck for hours or days, and the heartbeat reaches a PC session, not a person.
detect: The heartbeat's GONE QUIET marker; read only if a PC session starts.
response: 1. Look at the heartbeat. 2. Log in to the Mac and run the checker by hand. 3. Re-authenticate GitLab.
smallest_fix: Copy the GONE QUIET condition into the GitHub alarm email so a phone sees it.

event: A bug ships in an App Store build and there is no way to turn it off or tell old builds to update, because the front end is bundled and no minimum-version or kill switch exists.
trigger: Any bad app release, or any server change that breaks an older installed build. The API base is fixed in each binary.
cost: A bad build stays on phones for days (Apple review plus user updates); old builds must stay compatible forever or users break.
detect: Users only; no version is reported to the server in a form anyone reads (not checked in full).
response: 1. Fix and submit with expedited review. 2. Keep the server compatible with the bad build. 3. Message users through the store notes.
smallest_fix: In the next build add a small server-checked minimum version and a 'please update' screen, plus a remote switch for risky features.
fix_cost: 3 hours, one more App Store release
sources: native/README.md; native/capacitor.config.json; app/public/js/flags.js (flags are compiled into the bundle)

event: A new iOS release or Apple's yearly minimum-SDK rule breaks the app or blocks new builds (webview, Keychain, camera barcode scanning, Capacitor version).
trigger: iOS 27 arrives around September 2027; Apple raises the required SDK each spring; Capacitor and plugin versions lag.
cost: Scanner or purchases break on updated phones; submissions blocked until a rebuild; one to three days of work at a bad time.
detect: Users on the beta iOS, reviews, or Apple's SDK-deadline email.
response: 1. Test on the new iOS beta in summer. 2. Update Capacitor and plugins. 3. Ship before the deadline.
smallest_fix: Calendar a September check and an April SDK check, and keep one test phone on each iOS beta.
fix_cost: 20 minutes setup, 4 to 8 hours per year

event: A change adds a new data use (a new vendor, a new field sent to a service, a new analytics event) and the privacy policy, App Store privacy label and Law 25 notice are not updated.
trigger: A feature merged by a quick push. The privacy and legal pages are separate hosted files.
cost: An Apple rejection or a complaint; mismatch with a published promise.
detect: Nobody would know until Apple or a user raises it.
response: 1. Compare the change with the policy. 2. Update the policy and the label. 3. Re-submit.
smallest_fix: Add one line to the deploy checklist: 'did this change what is collected or who gets it?'

event: The public store pages (privacy policy, terms, support) go down or get renamed, because they live under Jamin's personal GitHub name (xu826jamin.github.io/pexi); Apple needs working links.
trigger: A repo rename, the repo made private, a GitHub account change or Pages turned off.
cost: An app review problem or removal for a dead policy link; the personal name is also public in that web address.
detect: Nobody would know; the alarm does not fetch those pages (not checked in full).
response: 1. Restore the Pages site. 2. Re-point the App Store links. 3. Add the page to the alarm.
smallest_fix: Add the policy and support URLs to the alarm probe, and move them to the Pexi domain when one exists.

event: Nobody reads a weekly numbers page, so low hit rate, falling installs, subscription churn or a quiet success all go unnoticed.
trigger: Only 27 percent of 176 real scans had a shop price (NOW.md). The data exists (scan log, App Store Connect) but no routine reads it.
cost: Churn driven by 'no price' on 3 of 4 scans is invisible; a good week (or a collapse) goes unmanaged. The most likely slow leak of money.
detect: Nobody would know.
response: 1. Read installs, subscribers, cancellations and scan hit rate once a week. 2. Pick the one number that moved. 3. Act on it.
smallest_fix: A weekly email to Jamin from the server with scans, share with a shop price, free to Plus conversions and top unmatched barcodes; Jamin reads it for 10 minutes.
sources: NOW.md; app/server.ts (scan log and usage events)

event: Jamin starts the 16-month AMD internship on May 3, 2027 and the server, support and releases stop getting attention; he may also move city, leaving the Mac at home.
trigger: Full-time work, possible relocation, an employer outside-work or disclosure rule (not read, not a legal view).
cost: Every other gap on this list gets worse: unread email, unrenewed things, down server nobody restarts.
detect: It is a known date; no handover plan is recorded.
response: 1. Decide by April where the server lives. 2. Hand the weekly routine to a named person. 3. Check the employer's rules on side work.
smallest_fix: A one-page plan before April: who restarts the Mac, who reads email, whether to move the server to a rented machine with its own restarts.
fix_cost: 2 hours, 5 to 10 dollars a month if the server moves

event: The partnership is strained or Aurik leaves, is unavailable, or disagrees, and the French translation, store paperwork and shopper-side app ownership are left unsettled.
trigger: A year of unpaid or underpaid work; no written ownership or revenue agreement was found (not found, not proven absent). The App Store account is in Jamin's name; the shopper-side app is Aurik's.
cost: A stalled release, losing the French text and App Store know-how, or a dispute over money once there is revenue.
detect: Only through a conversation.
response: 1. Talk early. 2. Write down roles, split and what happens if either leaves. 3. Share account access in writing.
smallest_fix: One page covering roles, revenue split, account ownership and an exit rule, signed by both.

event: Another business named Pexi objects to the name, or another app takes the name or a lookalike in the App Store.
trigger: A launch makes the name visible; the trademark application was drafted and left unsubmitted.
cost: A forced rename after launch is expensive (the hostname and store identity are fixed); a cease-and-desist letter takes time.
detect: Only a letter or an App Store dispute email.
response: 1. Read the claim and note the dates. 2. Ask a lawyer. 3. Decide to hold, negotiate or rename.
smallest_fix: Re-run the name search before launch day and decide whether to file the draft.
fix_cost: 1 hour, filing fee about 491 dollars if filed
sources: RULINGS.md (Name: Pexi; CIPO draft left unsubmitted)

event: A French-speaking or Quebec user complains (missing French screens, English-only store listing or subscription terms, an English reply to a French email).
trigger: A bilingual app in Quebec; the Quebec rules and language expectations in the legal review.
cost: Complaints, an Office complaint risk, bad reviews from Quebec.
detect: Only through the support inbox (blind-14) or a review.
response: 1. Reply in French. 2. Fix the missing text in the next build. 3. Check the French store listing.
smallest_fix: Have Aurik walk through every screen and the store page in French once and list what is English.

event: A child or parent complains or a regulator asks about children's data, since the app is rated 4+ and open to all ages.
trigger: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner's children's privacy code; kids using a shopping app.
cost: Complaint handling time; possible policy changes; reputation.
detect: Only through the support inbox (blind-14).
response: 1. Reply politely. 2. Point to the policy and delete data on request. 3. Review the code's requirements.
smallest_fix: Add a short paragraph to the data-requests doc about requests made by or for a child.

event: Outreach to store contacts from the Mac's crawl job (contacts found and marked sendable) creates spam complaints or a reply flood nobody handles.
trigger: The mailbox shows a crawl job collecting store contacts. What the contacts will be used for was not checked; this item applies only if they are used for cold email.
cost: Canadian anti-spam law carries fines; replies from stores land in an unread inbox; a domain or Gmail account flagged.
detect: Complaint or a blocked account.
response: 1. Confirm the purpose of the list. 2. If emailing, include consent basis and unsubscribe. 3. Read replies weekly.
smallest_fix: Ask what the list is for before it is used and have a reply owner and unsubscribe path ready.

event: The TestFlight build expires (90 days) or the beta group loses access, so testers (Aurik, friends) cannot open the app while a public fix is waiting.
trigger: Build 9 uploaded 2026-11-17; TestFlight builds stop working after 90 days.
cost: Small: lose testers for a few days; the beta feedback loop breaks.
detect: Testers tell us.
response: 1. Upload a new build. 2. Re-invite testers.
smallest_fix: Calendar a reminder 80 days after each build.
